web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Syllabus Overview
web_content_rtb__content.value:
The Mathematics Standard 11–12 Syllabus aligns with the Mathematics Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus to provide opportunities for integrated delivery.

Through collaborative curriculum planning, it may be decided that Life Skills outcomes and content are the most appropriate option for some students with intellectual disability.

Organisation of Mathematics Standard 11–12

The organisation of outcomes and content for Mathematics Standard 11–12 highlights the important role Working mathematically plays across all areas of mathematics and reflects the strengthened connections between concepts. Working mathematically has been embedded in the outcomes and content of the syllabus.

Mathematics Standard 11–12 outcomes and their related content are organised into 5 areas of study:

  • Algebra
  • Financial mathematics
  • Measurement
  • Networks
  • Statistics.

Figure 1 shows the organisation of Mathematics Standard 11–12. All Year 11 Mathematics Standard focus areas are to be completed first, then focus areas from Year 12 Mathematics Standard 1 OR Year 12 Mathematics Standard 2 are to be completed.

Image long description: Five rows represent the areas of study for Mathematics Standard 11–12. Each row is divided into thirds, showing the focus areas for Year 11, Year 12 (Mathematics Standard 1) or Year 12 (Mathematics Standard 2). The Algebra area of study includes: Year 11 focus areas Formulas and equations and Linear relationships; the Year 12 (Standard 1) focus area Algebraic relationships; and the Year 12 (Standard 2) focus area Algebraic relationships. The Financial mathematics area of study includes: the Year 11 focus areas Earning money, and Managing money; the Year 12 (Standard 1) focus areas Investment, and Depreciation and loans; and the Year 12 (Standard 2) focus areas Investment and loans, and Annuities. The Measurement area of study includes: the Year 11 focus areas Applications of measurement, and Time and location; the Year 12 (Standard 1) focus areas Right-angled triangles, and Ratios and rates; and the Year 12 (Standard 2) focus areas Trigonometry, and Ratios and rates. The Networks area of study includes: the Year 11 focus area Networks, paths and trees; and the Year 12 (Standard 2) focus areas Network flow, and Critical path analysis. The Statistics area of study includes: the Year 11 focus area Data analysis; the Year 12 (Standard 1) focus areas Bivariate data analysis, and Relative frequency and probability; and the Year 12 (Standard 2) focus areas Bivariate data analysis, Relative frequency and probability, and The normal distribution. All content is surrounded by a box labelled with the phrase, ‘Working mathematically through communicating reasoning, understanding and fluency, and problem solving’.

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Mathematics Standard 11–12 focuses on enabling students to use mathematics to make informed decisions in their daily lives. Students develop understanding and competence through real-world applications of mathematics.

Mathematics Standard 1 provides opportunities for students to build confidence and make mathematics meaningful. Students develop their mathematical knowledge and understanding through applying and modelling to prepare for post-school employment or further training.

Mathematics Standard 2 provides a pathway for students to extend their mathematical thinking by examining more complex content, and through applications and modelling.

What students learn

Through the study of Mathematics Standard 1, students:

  • develop their knowledge, understanding and skills in Working mathematically and in communicating concisely and systematically
  • consider various applications of mathematics in a broad range of contemporary contexts through mathematical modelling and use these models to solve problems related to their present and future needs
  • gain an appropriate mathematical background for post-school employment or further training.

Through the study of Mathematics Standard 2, students:

  • develop their knowledge, understanding and skills in Working mathematically and in communicating concisely and systematically
  • consider various applications of mathematics in a broad range of contemporary contexts through mathematical modelling and use these models to solve problems related to their present and future needs
  • develop an understanding of, and skills in, further aspects of mathematics for concurrent HSC studies
  • gain an appropriate mathematical background for a wide range of educational and employment aspirations.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Mathematics Life Skills 11–12 provides opportunities for students to develop knowledge and understanding through real-world applications of mathematics. Students develop skills in using number and mathematics in daily life.

What students learn

Through the study of Mathematics Life Skills 11–12, students:

  • apply mathematical operations to practical situations and develop skills to solve everyday problems related to time, money, measurement, travel and probability
  • independently or collaboratively explore numeracy and mathematical thinking, knowledge and skills in an area of personal interest in the Mathematics project
  • apply mathematics in a variety of contexts to enhance and encourage participation in post-school contexts
  • apply knowledge, understanding and skills to everyday scenarios to solve problems, make real-world connections and prepare for a range of post-school pathways.

Course structure

Mathematics Life Skills Year 11 and Year 12

The following focus areas can be studied throughout Year 11 (120 hours) and Year 12 (120 hours):

  • Number
  • Financial mathematics
  • Measurement
  • Plans, maps and networks
  • Data, statistics and probability
  • Mathematics project.

For Mathematics Life Skills:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Mathematics Life Skills 11–12 outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the Mathematics Life Skills 11–12 outcomes and content and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • Skills from the overarching outcome, Working mathematically, are integrated throughout the course.
  • Content and examples focus on personal and real-world connections for post-school pathways.
  • The Mathematics project can be integrated into any aspect of the course or undertaken as a discrete focus area for students with specific mathematical interest areas. The project can be undertaken collaboratively or independently.
  • Examples provided in the content are suggestions only. Teachers may use the examples provided or use other examples to meet the particular needs of individual students.
Mathematics project

In the Mathematics project, students independently or collaboratively explore numeracy and mathematical thinking, knowledge and skills in an area of personal interest. This project can help students make connections between numeracy and their personal lives and also in their local or broader community, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities. Areas of interest may be related to a student’s home, school, community or workplace and/or be of relevance to employment, further education or training.

Students build on knowledge and skills from some or all of the focus areas. The Mathematics project is an opportunity for students to develop numerical reasoning skills as they transition from recalling mathematical facts and procedures to applying their knowledge and skills in an increasing range of contexts, especially in preparation for post-school pathways.

Mathematical thinking involves students’ consideration of different possibilities, providing opportunities for curiosity, creativity and thinking critically. Students can investigate a topic of interest with mathematical relevance by identifying the problem or scenario and approaching the project from a mathematical point of view. Students can connect the information to prior or new knowledge, and collect, organise and present their findings.

The Mathematics project is optional. The learning activities undertaken will be determined by the interests and learning needs of students. Students can follow all or selected parts of the process outlined in this focus area. The process should be differentiated in modes of representation and communication of findings. The delivery of the project should reflect the level of autonomy of the students – for example, undertaking the Mathematics project may involve a series of short tasks, or one or more longer projects.

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Mathematics Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus.

examples.value:

A cylinder is round and has a top and bottom in the shape of a circle. The top and bottom are flat and always the same size. There are no vertices (corners).

A cone has a single flat face (also called its base) that is in the shape of a circle. The body of the cone has curved sides that lead up to a narrow point at the top called a vertex (corner).

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

The focus area of Measurement provides opportunities for students to develop skills including telling the time so they are able to manage and plan for personal activities. Students identify 2D and 3D shapes and attributes from a range of contexts. They apply this knowledge to solve real-world problems that relate to length, area, volume, capacity and mass. Students also develop knowledge of temperatures and energy in order to make everyday decisions. The learning connects to activities including measuring everyday items, food preparation, storage of items and energy consumption.

Considerations

Teachers may consider addressing the content at different times during the course. For example, time could be studied independently to content related to shapes and measuring temperature and energy, and related applications could be combined in a further unit of study.

Explicitly teaching the meaning of subject-specific terms and mathematical symbols is important to support all learners. Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Key terms for this focus area include:

  • year
  • hour
  • minute
  • fortnight
  • second
  • week
  • month
  • digital
  • analog
  • perimeter
  • length
  • width
  • height
  • area
  • squared
  • surface area
  • pronumerals
  • cubed
  • volume
  • weight
  • temperature
  • mass
  • capacity
  • energy
  • 2-dimensional
  • 3-dimensional
  • scale
  • flat
  • curved
  • pointed
  • shape
  • face
  • edge
  • vertices.

Problem solving and use of examples from every day activities are important to support students to make real-world applications and connections of relevance.

Teaching and learning

Below are examples of teaching strategies to support student learning.

Using a range of concrete objects or manipulatives. For example:

  • Analog measuring tools such as rulers, tape measures, string, spoons, cups, buckets, scales, clocks and trundle wheels.
  • Digital measuring tools such as watches, mobile phones, stopwatches, online calendars and digital diaries.
  • Everyday items with measurement displays such as ovens, fridges, air conditioners, thermometers and cars.
  • Using handspans or blocks to informally measure a small object such as the length of a book or table in the classroom.
  • Assembling 3-dimensional items such as a table, cupboard or bookcase.
  • Arranging physical items from lightest to heaviest.

Sequencing learning. For example:

  • Providing opportunities for students to identify and describe shapes before performing calculations or operations based on the features of shapes. Illustrative tasks include:
    • Identification tasks such as identifying shapes in nature, the home, the classroom, built structures, equipment, tools and devices, in pictures, images and online.
    • Descriptive tasks such as describing features of a shape from an image, ‘A square has 4 equal sides. Each side is 5 cm long. The perimeter of the square is 20 cm’.
    • Calculation tasks such as using the concept that opposite sides of a rectangle are equal to calculate the perimeter of a rectangle given the length and width.

Explicitly teaching connections between concepts. For example:

  • The equivalence between different representations of time such as 11 o’clock, 11 pm and 23:00 hours.

Scaffolding the steps required to solve problems. For example:

  • The train departs from the station at 10.55 am and arrives at its destination after 2 hours and 15 minutes. At what time did the train reach its destination?
  • A large box has a mass of 25 kilograms. A small box has a mass of 14 kilograms. What is the difference in mass between the large and small box?
    • Use physical objects of different masses to compare mass.
    • Use images or large and small boxes and have students place the labels of ‘25 kilograms’ and ‘14 kilograms’ on the appropriate box.
    • Use comparative language such as more than and less than to identify that the large box has a mass more than the small box.
    • Identify that difference is found by subtracting the small mass from the large mass.
    • Use visual aids, such as number lines or counting objects to demonstrate subtraction.
    • Subtract the small mass from the large mass.

Connecting with Mathematics Standard 11–12

This focus area aligns with the measurement areas of study in Mathematics Standard 11–12:

  • Year 11: Applications of measurement; Time and location
  • Year 12 Standard 1: Right-angled triangles; Ratios and rates
  • Year 12 Standard 2: Trigonometry; Ratios and rates

The following table provides examples of connections between Mathematics Life Skills and Mathematics Standard.

Mathematics Standard 11–12Mathematics Life Skills 11–12
In Applications of measurement (Year 11) students recognise and convert metric units of measure and calculate perimeter, area and volume. This includes complex shapes and solids such as calculating areas of irregularly shaped blocks of land.Students recognise and convert metric units of measure and calculate perimeter, area and volume. Students may focus on area calculations for squares and rectangles.
In Time and location (Year 11) students may develop skills in understanding 24-hour time and applying it to read and interpret timetables. Students calculate elapsed time for a range of problems.Students may develop skills in understanding 24-hour time and applying it to read and interpret timetables. Students may focus on calculations such as travel time.

Purpose

The focus area of Number provides opportunities for students to build foundational knowledge and skills in numeracy. The content allows students to connect their learning to everyday observations and activities and build problem-solving skills that can be used in a range of contexts. Numeracy knowledge and skills support students in decision-making such as for money management, purchasing goods and services, travel and food preparation.

Considerations

Number may be an effective and appropriate initial area of study as it emphasises the foundational knowledge and skills that support mathematical learning in all focus areas. The content supports learning throughout the course and can be integrated with other focus areas or revisited. The understanding of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division is foundational. Using these functions in algorithms provides opportunities for students to develop number skills of counting, categorising and calculating with whole and parts of integers.

Explicitly teaching the meaning of subject-specific terms and mathematical symbols is important to support all learners. Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Key terms for this focus area include:

  • decrease
  • increase
  • ascend
  • descend
  • value
  • add
  • subtract
  • multiply
  • divide
  • plus
  • minus
  • difference
  • product
  • quotient
  • operation
  • equals
  • equivalent
  • zero
  • integer
  • compare
  • order
  • count
  • fractions
  • decimals
  • percentages
  • denominator
  • numerator
  • half
  • quarter
  • third
  • tenth
  • hundredth
  • thousandth.

Problem solving and use of examples are important to support students to make real-world applications and connections of relevance.

Teaching and learning  

Below are examples of teaching strategies to support student learning.

Using a range of concrete objects or manipulatives. For example:

  • Counters, blocks or everyday items such as straws and beads to represent number.
  • Number cards, strips and tactile representations.
  • Games such as dominoes and cards.

Explicitly teaching connections between concepts. For example:

Providing worked examples and models. For example:

  • Using accounts, bills, receipts and phone plans to model calculations and interpret numerical data.
  • Using sketches, diagrams or algorithms to demonstrate how positive and negative numbers correspond to temperatures in various locations.
  • Calculating the cost and discount of an item of clothing that is on sale.
  • Breaking down the charges listed on a bill or receipt using a number grid or spreadsheet to illustrate the individual cost of each item or service.
  • Using video modelling to demonstrate counting on by selected amounts.

Providing wait time to allow for students to process numerical information. For example:

  • Providing students with a set of decimals such as 27.27, 4.12, 27.77, 39.01, 4.18 and allowing sufficient wait time before asking students to arrange the set into a decreasing order.
  • Using coloured cards or objects that students can display to indicate they are ready to provide a response.

Connecting with Mathematics Standard 11–12

Number is a foundational focus area in Mathematics Life Skills. It can be integrated with other focus areas in Mathematics Life Skills and connects to each of the focus areas in Mathematics Standard 11–12.

The following table provides examples of connections between Mathematics Life Skills and Mathematics Standard.

In Applications of measurement (Year 11) students identify and convert between the metric units of length.Students recognise, compare and order numbers in a range of contexts.

Purpose

In the Mathematics project, students explore an area of interest with numerical and mathematical relevance. The project provides opportunities to revisit and consolidate prior learning and can be used to integrate concepts and skills from more than one focus area. The focus area may support students’ self-awareness through reflection on strengths and interests and support the development of resilience and a sense of achievement and success. It may challenge and extend students at their level and pace. The focus area can promote curiosity and confidence to make learning gains in Mathematics. It may engage and motivate students by providing an opportunity for them to investigate something of personal significance.

Considerations

Students can complete one or more mathematics projects over the course. A project could be a short task at the end of a focus area that consolidates and uses the concepts and skills taught. It could be an extended investigation or ongoing project that students work on for one or more periods each week, or it could be set as an independent or collaborative task to be completed during assessment periods such as the trial HSC.

Teachers have the flexibility to plan projects with students that best address their individual strengths, needs and interests, as well as the context and resourcing of the setting.

Ideas for topics are included as prompts but are not exhaustive or directive. Ideas can also be drawn from connections with other subjects being studied, areas of interest and involvement, or to address a need from outside school that may be identified through the individualised planning process. Student choice should be an integral part of the project.

The Mathematics project may incorporate knowledge and skills from multiple focus areas.  Depending on the nature of the project, outcomes and content from other focus areas may be selected and integrated with this focus area. Teachers should consider outcomes and content that align with the student's interests and that challenge and extend the students while learning about a topic.

The Mathematics project provides multiple opportunities for quality differentiated instruction when considering:

  • student levels of progress and attainment in mathematics, numeracy and literacy
  • learning preferences or communication form(s)
  • potential for whole class or small group activities
  • available support for independent or group work.

The project is an opportunity for the student to showcase their skills and knowledge. The project should provide evidence to the both the teacher and student of acquisition of new or developed learning about mathematics and numeracy related to the topic.

Students completing the project should be supported on an ongoing basis and to the extent required to facilitate progress with the investigative process. Scaffolds or adjustments can be used. The teacher should facilitate opportunities for students to recall, revise and relearn foundational numerical knowledge and skills. Materials used, collected and presented should be accessible and in a range of modes.

The language of mathematics is meaningful and can be the doorway to applying numerical knowledge and mathematical skills to everyday activities and real-world applications safely and competently. Linking mathematical language to scenarios, and introducing, explaining, using accurately, and modelling mathematical language are all vital in the project.

Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Teaching and learning

Considerations for project options could include:

Focus areaProject options
Number
  • Collate information about belongings by setting up a spreadsheet.
  • Design a decoration for a public space using a tessellation or pattern.
  • Design a recreational area using percentages. For example, the area must be at least 60% open space and no more than 10% concrete.
Financial mathematics
  • Compare and choose from a range of mobile phone plans.
  • Investigate available plans for commonly used services such as home internet or streaming services.
  • Investigate a range of financial products to use for personal financial management.
  • Set up a budget spreadsheet for personal finances or a payment schedule for expenses.
  • Plan an event such as a class celebration.
  • Investigate buying a car: research different cars, what is affordable, the upfront and ongoing costs associated with running a car.
  • Explore the costs of living out of home.
Measurement
  • Design a dog park.
  • Redesign a room.
  • Organise an annual birthday and events calendar.
  • Plan and schedule a trip to a nearby venue using public transport, considering opening hours, dates and travel times.
Plans, maps and networks
  • Plan a class excursion in the local area using maps and timetables.
  • Plan a trip to an event with friends or family.
  • Plan an overnight or longer holiday.
  • Use scale plans of a property to design an extension to the house, or plan gardens and paddocks for the land.
Data, statistics and probability
  • Collect, display and analyse data about an industry or workplace to help make decisions relating to a future job or career.
  • Conduct probability investigations to explore a topic of interest.
  • Gather, display and analyse the statistics for a favourite sporting team.

Connecting with Mathematics Standard 11–12

The Mathematics project may align with any relevant focus areas in Mathematics Standard 11–12. The following table provides examples of connections between Mathematics Life Skills and Mathematics Standard.

Mathematics Standard 11–12Mathematics Life Skills 11–12

In Applications of measurement (Year 11) students convert between units of measurement and explore perimeter and surface area.


A student undertaking a project to design an outdoor recreational space may address content from the Mathematics project together with content from the Number and Measurement focus areas. They may measure the perimeter of the outdoor space in metres.
In Investment (Year 12) and Depreciation and loans (Year 12) students consider the financial implications of purchases over time, such as alternative investment of money, the depreciation of a purchased car over time and the ongoing impact of loans.A student undertaking a project to investigate buying a car may address content from the Mathematics project together with content from the Financial mathematics focus area. They may develop a budget that includes costs associated with buying a car.

Purpose

The collection and statistical analysis of data is of fundamental importance in society. Conclusions drawn from the statistical analysis of data are used to inform decisions made in government, science, business and industry. It is important that students have a broad understanding of how data and statistics are used, as well as how statistics are misused, resulting in the misrepresentation of information.

Considerations

  • Data that is current and relevant should be used when studying Data analysis. Students can develop their own datasets for analysis or use some of the datasets available online. Online data sources include the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) website.
  • The teacher should instruct students to avoid overlapping classes, ensuring that each class size is the same with no gaps between each interval, and how to calculate class centre. The analysis of grouped data requires calculation of the class centre.
  • When using a spreadsheet to organise and represent data and calculate measures of centre and spread, students should create tables, use basic functions with cell referencing and generate graphs. The following functions may be useful:
    • AVERAGE() Returns the average
    • COUNT() Counts how many numbers
    • MAX() Returns the maximum value
    • MEDIAN() Returns the median of the given numbers
    • MIN() Returns the minimum value
    • MODE() Returns the most common value in a data set
    • STDEV.P() Calculates standard deviation based on the entire population
    • SUM() Returns the total of the selected range of cell values

Considerations

  • Goods and services tax (GST) calculations should include finding the GST amount, the final cost, and finding the original cost of goods before GST was added.
  • Buy now, pay later services are becoming more common as a payment option for many consumer goods and services. Teachers could give examples that include calculating the total cost of using one of these services including the cost of setting up one of these accounts, the payment instalments and any late payment fees.
  • Buying on terms is another way to pay for many goods and services, including vehicles. Teachers could give examples that include calculating the total cost of using one of these services, including paying a deposit and the payment instalments. The total cost of this could be compared to paying the entire price upfront.
  • When calculating the cost of a vehicle, examples could be used where the cost of registration and insurance is given in the question.
  • Stamp duty could be given as a flat rate or could be calculated using a sliding scale from a published table. Basic calculations involving fuel to estimate the ongoing costs of running a vehicle could be included. For example, a car with a 40 L tank will need to be refilled every two weeks and fuel costs 192.2 c/L.
  • When using a spreadsheet to model the costs of purchasing, running and maintaining a vehicle students could create tables and use basic spreadsheet functions with cell referencing. Students could compare the cost of purchasing a second-hand car with a new car, or a petrol car with an electric car. Students could generate graphs to communicate their findings.  
  • Use household documents including bills to interpret information about a household’s energy and resource usage and to make informed financial judgments and decisions. The use of solar panels and how this can contribute to a household’s energy efficiency could also be examined.
  • When using a spreadsheet to model budgets, teachers could give scenarios to students to create a budget and examine the impact of reducing or increasing spending.
  • Teachers could present scenarios where a person needs to pay off a debt or save money towards a goal, so students could compare different strategies to minimise financial problems such as monitoring spending and using a budget.

Purpose

Networks involve the graphical representation and modelling of situations as an approach to decision-making processes. Knowledge of networks enables development of a logical sequence of tasks or a clear understanding of connections between people or items.

ConnectionsCourse/Stage/Focus area
There are many applications of problems involving flows through networks, such as the movement of traffic through an airport, the flow of water in a system of pipes or the transfer of data across a computer intranet.Real-world applications

Considerations

  • Students should be supported to develop fluency in converting information between different representations of networks, for example, converting from a table to a diagram and vice versa.
  • A flow must obey two rules:
    • The flow assigned to an edge must lie between zero and the capacity of the edge.
    • The inflow of a vertex (total flow of incoming edges) must be equal to the outflow of a vertex (total flow of outgoing edges). This means that vertices cannot ‘store’ flow and are simply where edges meet.
  • In networks, saturated edges are those edges that have zero excess flow capacity.
  • The excess flow capacity of an edge is the difference between the flow through the edge and the capacity of the edge.
  • Knowledge of saturated edges can be used to support the calculation and analysis of the flow capacity of a network. This process is known as the ‘saturated edges method’.

Course/Stage/Focus area

The mean and standard deviation are used to calculate z-scores.

Mathematics Standard Year 11 Data analysis

The normal distribution often describes natural phenomena, such as the distribution of heights, in a population.

Scientists use the normal distribution and z-scores to assess the significance of experimental results and make conclusions about hypotheses.

Real-world applications

The normal distribution is used in psychology, particularly in psychological testing and assessments. Test scores, such as IQ or standardised test results, are often distributed normally, and psychologists use this distribution to interpret scores.

z-scores are used in psychological research to analyse survey data, test scores and behavioural data, in order to draw conclusions and make psychological assessments.

Real-world applications

The normal distribution is applied in healthcare and medicine. For example, vital signs like blood pressure, cholesterol levels and body temperatures often follow a normal distribution, allowing healthcare professionals to set diagnostic thresholds and assess patient health.

Real-world applications

Engineers use the normal distribution in quality control and manufacturing processes. Deviations from a desired specification can be analysed using the normal distribution to ensure product quality.

Real-world applications

The normal distribution and z-scores are used in advanced data analysis, including hypothesis testing, confidence intervals and statistical inference.

  • Student understanding of formulas can be supported by teaching formulas within the context of targeted questions. Emphasis should be placed on using and manipulating formulas, not on memorisation.
  • Substitution of numbers into algebraic expressions and equations should include expressions containing multiple variables, positive and negative values, powers and square roots.
  • Formulas that are used in subsequent focus areas could be used in this focus area to demonstrate substitution, evaluation and changing the subject.
  • When using formulas, students may benefit from examining how to solve an equation using a formula involving up to two algebraic fractions. For example, in Mathematics Standard 2 Trigonometry, the sine rule has two algebraic fractions.
  • Reaction time is the time period from when a driver decides to brake to when the driver first commences braking.
  • Different formulas exist for calculating reaction distance and braking distance. Students should have opportunities to solve problems using different formulas involving different speeds, road conditions and weather conditions.
  • To assist students in translating word problems to linear equations, words related to common operations should be taught explicitly. For example: sum (+), of (×), difference (-), shared (÷).
  • When using a spreadsheet to dynamically calculate using formulas, students should become fluent in using basic mathematical operations with cell referencing. Basic mathematical operations include addition (+), multiplication (*), subtraction (–) and division (/). For example: =(10*F5-7.5*F6)/(5.5*F7)

• Students may have seen the symbol for the mean as x ‾ (this is commonly used on scientific calculators). In the formula for the z-score, the Greek letter mu, μ is used for the mean.
  • Initially, students should explore z-scores from a pictorial perspective, investigating only whole number multiples of the standard deviation.
  • The importance of z-scores can be explained with the following:
    • raw scores by themselves do not necessarily provide information about the position in a distribution
    • standardising different distributions allows us to make comparisons between these distributions.
  • The advantages of using standardised scores can be explored by comparing two or more sets of scores before and after conversion to z-scores.
  • Graphical representations of datasets before and after standardisation should be explored.
  • When examining z-scores and probability, the empirical rule can be used to estimate probabilities for data points falling within one, two, or three standard deviations of the mean. While statistical tables can be used to determine probabilities for any z-score, this level of precision is not essential for Mathematics Standard 2.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

The focus area of Data, statistics and probability provides opportunities for students to explore data in a range of contexts and consider the purposes of data representations including the use of data in advertising and educational materials. Students may apply their understanding of data to develop independence and inform decision-making. This includes decisions related to daily living and money management. Students may develop critical thinking by exploring gambling in society and examining the mathematics of chance.

Considerations

Explicitly teaching the meaning of subject-specific terms and mathematical symbols is important to support all learners. Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Key terms for this focus area include:

  • data
  • bias
  • selection
  • graphs
  • tables
  • pictograms
  • infographics
  • tally
  • score
  • skew
  • misleading
  • chance
  • probability
  • certain
  • impossible
  • frequency
  • likely
  • theoretical
  • experiment
  • results
  • findings
  • conclusions
  • gambling
  • gambler’s fallacy.

Problem solving and use of examples are important to support students to make real-world applications and connections of relevance.

Teaching and learning

Below are examples of teaching strategies to support student learning.

Using a range of concrete objects or manipulatives. For example:

  • Investigating chance and probability by rolling a die, tossing a coin, drawing a card from a deck of cards, using a spinner or drawing coloured marbles from a bag.
  • Displaying data using blocks or beads to create histograms or bar graphs.
  • Placing blocks, counters or objects representing different events on a 3D probability scale.

Feedback to guide next steps in the continuum of learning. For example:

  • Using student predictions about an event such as tossing a coin to provide feedback about the difference between probability and the results of experiments then reinforcing through repetition of predicting, experimenting and providing feedback.

Task analysis to sequence tasks and provide scaffolded instruction. For example, provide scaffolding and stepped instructions to locate, then collect, organise, represent and communicate data.

Using digital tools to develop digital skills. For example:

  • Using graphs and tables generated by spreadsheets or online tools to calculate the statistical probability of winning a lottery, the odds for sporting events and the insurance premiums for high-risk activities.
  • Using or creating an online infographic.
  • Participating in or conducting an online survey to collect data.

Connecting with Mathematics Standard 11–12

This focus area aligns with the statistics areas of study in Mathematics Standard 11–12:

  • Year 11: Data analysis
  • Year 12 Standard 1: Bivariate data analysis; Relative frequency and probability
  • Year 12 Standard 2: Bivariate data analysis; Relative frequency and probability; The normal distribution

The following table provides examples of connections between Mathematics Life Skills and Mathematics Standard.

Mathematics Standard 11–12Mathematics Life Skills 11–12
In Data analysis (Year 11) students recognise trends and patterns in data, draw inferences, and make generalisations and predictions. The complexity of the data, data display and statistical calculations will be more advanced for students in Mathematics Standard than in Mathematics Life Skills.

Students calculate the median, mode, range or standard deviation to draw conclusions about a dataset.

Students may recognise trends and patterns in data, draw inferences and make generalisations and predictions.

Students focus on interpreting aspects of the same data when it is displayed as a graph, table or infographic.


In Relative frequency and probability (Year 12) students have the opportunity to develop understanding of the range of probabilities from impossible to certain. Students model these probabilities using tools such as arrays and tree diagrams.Students have the opportunity to develop understanding of the range of probabilities from impossible to certain.

Students may communicate results from probability experiments using representations such as tallies and tables.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

The focus area of Financial mathematics provides opportunities for students to use money and make financial decisions in everyday contexts. By developing knowledge and skills related to earning, spending, saving and borrowing money students build independence and decision-making capabilities. These skills create opportunities for community participation in activities such as shopping and managing transportation expenses. This focus area also provides opportunities for students to explore a range of digital transactions and ways that money is used online. This content supports further development of money management skills including recognising dangers, scams and hidden costs to support safe online spending.

Considerations

Explicitly teaching the meaning of subject-specific terms and mathematical symbols is important to support all learners. Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Key terms for this focus area include:

  • financial institution
  • Automatic Teller Machine (ATM)
  • bank
  • cash
  • credit
  • debit
  • denominations
  • exchange rates
  • depreciation
  • savings
  • interest
  • earning
  • budget
  • currency
  • income
  • pay
  • debt
  • repayment
  • deductions
  • taxation
  • goods and services tax (GST)
  • net
  • gross
  • cost
  • purchases
  • digital
  • online
  • goods
  • services
  • consumer
  • Tax File Number (TFN)
  • investment
  • security
  • transactions.

Problem solving and use of examples are important to support students to make real-world applications and connections of relevance.

Teaching and learning

Below are examples of teaching strategies to support student learning.

Using a range of concrete objects or manipulatives. For example:

  • Notes and coins for counting and sorting, calculating using the 4 operations, budgeting and role-play activities.
  • A balance scale to represent the concept of a balanced budget.

Activating prior learning by connecting to everyday contexts. For example:

  • Exploring other currencies which may be relevant to student backgrounds.
  • Examining price lists from the local area such as menus, including money amounts written without end zeros (non-standard notation).
  • Using images of fuel prices at a local petrol station to interpret the amount in dollars and cents.
  • Surveying familiar people to identify reasons for borrowing money, such as buying or renovating a home, an overseas holiday, debt consolidation, moving expenses, car purchase, education or attending a major event.
  • Using relevant examples to make informed budgeting decisions based on available funds and future expenses, for example food is a need, but eating out in a restaurant is a want. I may want to spend money on going out, but I need to make sure I can pay my phone bill first.

Using digital tools for financial activities. For example:

  • Online budgeting tools to create a household budget.
  • Applications for banking to check balances and transfer money electronically.

Purpose

The focus area of Measurement provides opportunities for students to develop skills including telling the time so they are able to manage and plan for personal activities. Students identify 2D and 3D shapes and attributes from a range of contexts. They apply this knowledge to solve real-world problems that relate to length, area, volume, capacity and mass. Students also develop knowledge of temperatures and energy in order to make everyday decisions. The learning connects to activities including measuring everyday items, food preparation, storage of items and energy consumption.

Considerations

Teachers may consider addressing the content at different times during the course. For example, time could be studied independently to content related to shapes and measuring temperature and energy, and related applications could be combined in a further unit of study.

Explicitly teaching the meaning of subject-specific terms and mathematical symbols is important to support all learners. Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Key terms for this focus area include:

  • year

  • digital

  • energy
  • 2-dimensional

  • flat

  • pointed
  • shape
  • face
  • edge
  • vertices.

Problem solving and use of examples from every day activities are important to support students to make real-world applications and connections of relevance.

Teaching and learning

Below are examples of teaching strategies to support student learning.

Using a range of concrete objects or manipulatives. For example:

  • Analog measuring tools such as rulers, tape measures, string, spoons, cups, buckets, scales, clocks and trundle wheels.
  • Digital measuring tools such as watches, mobile phones, stopwatches, online calendars and digital diaries.
  • Everyday items with measurement displays such as ovens, fridges, air conditioners, thermometers and cars.
  • Using handspans or blocks to informally measure a small object such as the length of a book or table in the classroom.
  • Assembling 3-dimensional items such as a table, cupboard or bookcase.
  • Arranging physical items from lightest to heaviest.

Sequencing learning. For example:

  • Providing opportunities for students to identify and describe shapes before performing calculations or operations based on the features of shapes. Illustrative tasks include:
    • Identification tasks such as identifying shapes in nature, the home, the classroom, built structures, equipment, tools and devices, in pictures, images and online.
    • Descriptive tasks such as describing features of a shape from an image, ‘A square has 4 equal sides. Each side is 5 cm long. The perimeter of the square is 20 cm’.
    • Calculation tasks such as using the concept that opposite sides of a rectangle are equal to calculate the perimeter of a rectangle given the length and width.

Explicitly teaching connections between concepts. For example:

  • The equivalence between different representations of time such as 11 o’clock, 11 pm and 23:00 hours.

Scaffolding the steps required to solve problems. For example:

  • The train departs from the station at 10.55 am and arrives at its destination after 2 hours and 15 minutes. At what time did the train reach its destination?
  • A large box has a mass of 25 kilograms. A small box has a mass of 14 kilograms. What is the difference in mass between the large and small box?
    • Use physical objects of different masses to compare mass.
    • Use images or large and small boxes and have students place the labels of ‘25 kilograms’ and ‘14 kilograms’ on the appropriate box.
    • Use comparative language such as more than and less than to identify that the large box has a mass more than the small box.
    • Identify that difference is found by subtracting the small mass from the large mass.
    • Use visual aids, such as number lines or counting objects to demonstrate subtraction.
    • Subtract the small mass from the large mass.

Purpose

The focus area of Number provides opportunities for students to build foundational knowledge and skills in numeracy. The content allows students to connect their learning to everyday observations and activities and build problem-solving skills that can be used in a range of contexts. Numeracy knowledge and skills support students in decision-making such as for money management, purchasing goods and services, travel and food preparation.

Considerations

Number may be an effective and appropriate initial area of study as it emphasises the foundational knowledge and skills that support mathematical learning in all focus areas. The content supports learning throughout the course and can be integrated with other focus areas or revisited. The understanding of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division is foundational. Using these functions in algorithms provides opportunities for students to develop number skills of counting, categorising and calculating with whole and parts of integers.

Explicitly teaching the meaning of subject-specific terms and mathematical symbols is important to support all learners. Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Key terms for this focus area include:

  • decrease

Problem solving and use of examples are important to support students to make real-world applications and connections of relevance.

Teaching and learning  

Below are examples of teaching strategies to support student learning.

Using a range of concrete objects or manipulatives. For example:

  • Counters, blocks or everyday items such as straws and beads to represent number.
  • Number cards, strips and tactile representations.
  • Games such as dominoes and cards.

Explicitly teaching connections between concepts. For example:

Providing worked examples and models. For example:

  • Using accounts, bills, receipts and phone plans to model calculations and interpret numerical data.
  • Using sketches, diagrams or algorithms to demonstrate how positive and negative numbers correspond to temperatures in various locations.
  • Calculating the cost and discount of an item of clothing that is on sale.
  • Breaking down the charges listed on a bill or receipt using a number grid or spreadsheet to illustrate the individual cost of each item or service.
  • Using video modelling to demonstrate counting on by selected amounts.

Providing wait time to allow for students to process numerical information. For example:

  • Providing students with a set of decimals such as 27.27, 4.12, 27.77, 39.01, 4.18 and allowing sufficient wait time before asking students to arrange the set into a decreasing order.
  • Using coloured cards or objects that students can display to indicate they are ready to provide a response.

Connecting with Mathematics Standard 11–12

Number is a foundational focus area in Mathematics Life Skills. It can be integrated with other focus areas in Mathematics Life Skills and connects to each of the focus areas in Mathematics Standard 11–12.

Purpose

In the Mathematics project, students explore an area of interest with numerical and mathematical relevance. The project provides opportunities to revisit and consolidate prior learning and can be used to integrate concepts and skills from more than one focus area. The focus area may support students’ self-awareness through reflection on strengths and interests and support the development of resilience and a sense of achievement and success. It may challenge and extend students at their level and pace. The focus area can promote curiosity and confidence to make learning gains in Mathematics. It may engage and motivate students by providing an opportunity for them to investigate something of personal significance.

Considerations

Students can complete one or more mathematics projects over the course. A project could be a short task at the end of a focus area that consolidates and uses the concepts and skills taught. It could be an extended investigation or ongoing project that students work on for one or more periods each week, or it could be set as an independent or collaborative task to be completed during assessment periods such as the trial HSC.

Teachers have the flexibility to plan projects with students that best address their individual strengths, needs and interests, as well as the context and resourcing of the setting.

Ideas for topics are included as prompts but are not exhaustive or directive. Ideas can also be drawn from connections with other subjects being studied, areas of interest and involvement, or to address a need from outside school that may be identified through the individualised planning process. Student choice should be an integral part of the project.

The Mathematics project may incorporate knowledge and skills from multiple focus areas.  Depending on the nature of the project, outcomes and content from other focus areas may be selected and integrated with this focus area. Teachers should consider outcomes and content that align with the student's interests and that challenge and extend the students while learning about a topic.

The Mathematics project provides multiple opportunities for quality differentiated instruction when considering:

  • student levels of progress and attainment in mathematics, numeracy and literacy
  • learning preferences or communication form(s)
  • potential for whole class or small group activities
  • available support for independent or group work.

The project is an opportunity for the student to showcase their skills and knowledge. The project should provide evidence to the both the teacher and student of acquisition of new or developed learning about mathematics and numeracy related to the topic.

Students completing the project should be supported on an ongoing basis and to the extent required to facilitate progress with the investigative process. Scaffolds or adjustments can be used. The teacher should facilitate opportunities for students to recall, revise and relearn foundational numerical knowledge and skills. Materials used, collected and presented should be accessible and in a range of modes.

The language of mathematics is meaningful and can be the doorway to applying numerical knowledge and mathematical skills to everyday activities and real-world applications safely and competently. Linking mathematical language to scenarios, and introducing, explaining, using accurately, and modelling mathematical language are all vital in the project.

Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Teaching and learning

Considerations for project options could include:

Focus areaProject options
Number
  • Collate information about belongings by setting up a spreadsheet.
  • Design a decoration for a public space using a tessellation or pattern.
  • Design a recreational area using percentages. For example, the area must be at least 60% open space and no more than 10% concrete.
Financial mathematics
  • Compare and choose from a range of mobile phone plans.
  • Investigate available plans for commonly used services such as home internet or streaming services.
  • Investigate a range of financial products to use for personal financial management.
  • Set up a budget spreadsheet for personal finances or a payment schedule for expenses.
  • Plan an event such as a class celebration.
  • Investigate buying a car: research different cars, what is affordable, the upfront and ongoing costs associated with running a car.
  • Explore the costs of living out of home.
Measurement
  • Design a dog park.
  • Redesign a room.
  • Organise an annual birthday and events calendar.
  • Plan and schedule a trip to a nearby venue using public transport, considering opening hours, dates and travel times.
Plans, maps and networks
  • Plan a class excursion in the local area using maps and timetables.
  • Plan a trip to an event with friends or family.
  • Plan an overnight or longer holiday.
  • Use scale plans of a property to design an extension to the house, or plan gardens and paddocks for the land.
Data, statistics and probability
  • Collect, display and analyse data about an industry or workplace to help make decisions relating to a future job or career.
  • Conduct probability investigations to explore a topic of interest.
  • Gather, display and analyse the statistics for a favourite sporting team.

Connecting with Mathematics Standard 11–12

The Mathematics project may align with any relevant focus areas in Mathematics Standard 11–12. The following table provides examples of connections between Mathematics Life Skills and Mathematics Standard.

Mathematics Standard 11–12Mathematics Life Skills 11–12

In Applications of measurement (Year 11) students convert between units of measurement and explore perimeter and surface area.


A student undertaking a project to design an outdoor recreational space may address content from the Mathematics project together with content from the Number and Measurement focus areas. They may measure the perimeter of the outdoor space in metres.
In Investment (Year 12) and Depreciation and loans (Year 12) students consider the financial implications of purchases over time, such as alternative investment of money, the depreciation of a purchased car over time and the ongoing impact of loans.A student undertaking a project to investigate buying a car may address content from the Mathematics project together with content from the Financial mathematics focus area. They may develop a budget that includes costs associated with buying a car.

Purpose

In the focus area of Plans, maps and networks students learn about position, angles and scale. Students have opportunities to use maps and plans in real-world contexts, such as mapping travel routes and networks which are personally relevant. This can extend to examining local and global travel and movement routes and networks. This learning supports the development of independence and decision-making and provides skills to support active community participation and travel.

Considerations

The focus area of Plans, maps and networks may be taught in conjunction with other focus areas such as Number, Measurement and Financial mathematics. For example, students may apply their knowledge of fractions and decimals to understand ratio and scale, or apply their knowledge of measurement including calculating distances and time periods to travel.

Explicitly teaching the meaning of subject-specific terms and mathematical symbols is important to support all learners. Students for whom English is an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require additional support and targeted strategies to support their learning of language in relation to mathematics.

Key terms for this focus area include:

  • position
  • location
  • direction
  • compass
  • grid
  • scale
  • angles
  • ratio
  • rate
  • proportional
  • enlarge
  • reduce
  • plans
  • location
  • distance
  • networks
  • travel
  • connections
  • pathways
  • route
  • sequence.

Problem solving and use of examples are important to support students to make real-world applications and connections of relevance.

Teaching and learning

Below are examples of teaching strategies to support student learning.

Using a range of concrete objects or manipulatives. For example:

  • Notes and coins, a compass, tactile or 3D plans, and models.
  • Objects that can be moved in response to directional language such as:
    • A book that could be placed on top of, beside or underneath the table.
    • A block that can be moved left, right, forward and backward.

Activating prior learning by connecting to everyday contexts. For example:

  • Exploring plans of a familiar building or maps of the local area.
  • Using a compass to explore a local area.
  • Using familiar train networks and schedules to solve problems related to travelling to places of interest.
  • Using local road networks to plan the best route between 2 places on a local map.
  • Calculating distance and time taken for a familiar journey.

Sequencing learning. For example:

  • Providing opportunities for students to identify features of plans, maps and networks before performing calculations or solving problems. Illustrative tasks include:
    • Identification of key features on a map including landmarks, streets and intersections.
    • Identification of key features on a train network diagram including stations and intersections with other lines
    • Identification of key features of a building plan including rooms, doors and windows, such as:
      • Describing distances between places on a map as close or far away.
      • Describing train stations as on the same line or on a different line.
      • Describing rooms in a building as large or small.
      • Calculating distances between 2 places on a map.
      • Calculating the time to travel between 2 train stations.
      • Solving problems such as finding the shortest route between 2 points on a map.
      • Solving problems such as finding the largest room in a building.

Connecting with Mathematics Standard 11–12

This focus area aligns with the following focus areas in Mathematics Standard 11–12:

  • Year 11: Networks, paths and trees
  • Year 12 Standard 2: Network flow; Critical path analysis

Purpose

The collection and statistical analysis of data is of fundamental importance in society. Conclusions drawn from the statistical analysis of data are used to inform decisions made in government, science, business and industry. It is important that students have a broad understanding of how data and statistics are used, as well as how statistics are misused, resulting in the misrepresentation of information.

Prior knowledge, skills and understanding

  • classifying, displaying and interpreting data in graphical representations

  • interpreting the effect of individual data points on measures of centre and range
  • analysing datasets presented in various ways and drawing conclusions.

Related Stage 5 Core content

  • Mathematics Stage 5 Data analysis A

Related Stage 5 Path content

  • Mathematics Stage 5 Data analysis C (Path)

Making connections

Considerations

  • Data that is current and relevant should be used when studying Data analysis. Students can develop their own datasets for analysis or use some of the datasets available online. Online data sources include the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) website.
  • The teacher should instruct students to avoid overlapping classes, ensuring that each class size is the same with no gaps between each interval, and how to calculate class centre. The analysis of grouped data requires calculation of the class centre.
  • When using a spreadsheet to organise and represent data and calculate measures of centre and spread, students should create tables, use basic functions with cell referencing and generate graphs. The following functions may be useful:
    • AVERAGE() Returns the average
    • COUNT() Counts how many numbers
    • MAX() Returns the maximum value
    • MEDIAN() Returns the median of the given numbers
    • MIN() Returns the minimum value
    • MODE() Returns the most common value in a data set
    • STDEV.P() Calculates standard deviation based on the entire population
    • SUM() Returns the total of the selected range of cell values

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities in Data analysis

  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Ranger groups collect and analyse data, such as to identify and monitor animal and plant populations and water quality.
  • Data can be used to represent a range of information about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, Histories and Cultures, such as maintenance and revival of languages over time, and success of Community-controlled health initiatives and Aboriginal-owned enterprises.

Considerations

  • Learning and teaching in this topic should be supported by using real and current data. For example, calculations of wages and salaries should include calculations in relation to current awards and work contracts.
  • Government payments are an aspect of earning money. Government payments include payments that are relevant to students. Payment rates are often presented in tabular form and students are required to locate the necessary information based on a given context and calculate the required payment.
  • Students should calculate tax payable, including Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG) income tax and the Medicare levy, from current published tax tables.
  • Allowable tax deductions can include work-related expenses, travel expenses and donations to registered charities. Students should refer to current taxation information and consider tax deductions for different occupations.
  • When using a spreadsheet to model an employee’s income and taxation students should create tables and use basic spreadsheet functions with cell referencing. Students could practise changing pay rates or hours of work to examine the impact on an employee’s income. They might also generate graphs to compare different ways of earning. Taxation calculations could be completed to determine an employee’s net earnings in the PAYG taxation system.

  • The traditional sources of income for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples involved activities such as fishing, hunting, gathering, gardening and exchanging goods with other communities. Considerations

  • Goods and services tax (GST) calculations should include finding the GST amount, the final cost, and finding the original cost of goods before GST was added.
  • Buy now, pay later services are becoming more common as a payment option for many consumer goods and services. Teachers could give examples that include calculating the total cost of using one of these services including the cost of setting up one of these accounts, the payment instalments and any late payment fees.
  • Buying on terms is another way to pay for many goods and services, including vehicles. Teachers could give examples that include calculating the total cost of using one of these services, including paying a deposit and the payment instalments. The total cost of this could be compared to paying the entire price upfront.
  • When calculating the cost of a vehicle, examples could be used where the cost of registration and insurance is given in the question.
  • Stamp duty could be given as a flat rate or could be calculated using a sliding scale from a published table. Basic calculations involving fuel to estimate the ongoing costs of running a vehicle could be included. For example, a car with a 40 L tank will need to be refilled every two weeks and fuel costs 192.2 c/L.
  • When using a spreadsheet to model the costs of purchasing, running and maintaining a vehicle students could create tables and use basic spreadsheet functions with cell referencing. Students could compare the cost of purchasing a second-hand car with a new car, or a petrol car with an electric car. Students could generate graphs to communicate their findings.  
  • Use household documents including bills to interpret information about a household’s energy and resource usage and to make informed financial judgments and decisions. The use of solar panels and how this can contribute to a household’s energy efficiency could also be examined.

Purpose

Networks involve the graphical representation and modelling of situations as an approach to decision-making processes. Knowledge of networks enables development of a logical sequence of tasks or a clear understanding of connections between people or items.

Study of networks is important in developing students’ ability to interpret a set of connections or sequence of tasks as a concise diagram in order to solve related problems. Studying networks also develops students’ awareness of the applicability of networks throughout their lives (such as social networks) and their ability to use associated techniques to optimise practical problems.

Key terms

ConnectionsCourse/Stage/Focus area
There are many applications of problems involving flows through networks, such as the movement of traffic through an airport, the flow of water in a system of pipes or the transfer of data across a computer intranet.Real-world applications

Considerations

  • Students should be supported to develop fluency in converting information between different representations of networks, for example, converting from a table to a diagram and vice versa.
  • A flow must obey two rules:
    • The flow assigned to an edge must lie between zero and the capacity of the edge.
    • The inflow of a vertex (total flow of incoming edges) must be equal to the outflow of a vertex (total flow of outgoing edges). This means that vertices cannot ‘store’ flow and are simply where edges meet.
  • In networks, saturated edges are those edges that have zero excess flow capacity.
  • The excess flow capacity of an edge is the difference between the flow through the edge and the capacity of the edge.
  • Knowledge of saturated edges can be used to support the calculation and analysis of the flow capacity of a network. This process is known as the ‘saturated edges method’.

The collection and statistical analysis of data is of fundamental importance in society. Conclusions drawn from the statistical analysis of data are used to inform decisions made in government, science, business and industry. It is important that students have a broad understanding of how data and statistics are used, as well as how statistics are misused, resulting in the misrepresentation of information.

Purpose

Measurement involves the application of knowledge, understanding and skills of numbers and geometry to quantify and solve problems in practical situations. The study of measurement is important in developing students’ ability to solve problems related to two and three-dimensional models and representations.

The use of Pythagoras’ theorem and trigonometry in right-angled triangles has a range of applications in such fields as surveying, navigation, meteorology, architecture, construction and electronics.

Key terms

  • adjacent side
  • alternate angle
  • ambiguous case of the sine rule
  • angle of depression
  • angle of elevation
  • bearing
  • compass bearing
  • cosine ratio
  • cosine rule
  • degrees (geometry)
  • hypotenuse
  • minute (geometry)
  • obtuse angle
  • Pythagoras’ theorem
  • radial survey
  • sine ratio
  • sine rule
  • tangent ratio
  • trigonometric ratios
  • true bearing

Prior knowledge, skills and understanding

These concepts may be reviewed as required:

  • properties of angles formed by a transversal on parallel lines and basic angle properties
  • relevant notations and conventions for naming and labelling angles and triangles
  • classifying and using properties of triangles
  • using the angle sum of a triangle
  • solving numerical problems using properties of triangles
  • using degrees and minutes as a unit of measurement
  • compass directions
  • substitution into formulas
  • solving multi-step equations and equations involving fractions.

Related Stage 5 Core content

  • Mathematics Stage 5 Trigonometry A
  • Mathematics Stage 5 Trigonometry B

Related Stage 5 Path content

Making connections

ConnectionsCourse/Stage/Focus area
Rounding angles to the nearest degree, minute or second can be related to hours, minutes and seconds in time.Mathematics Standard Year 11 Time and location
Geometric shapes are used in design, architecture and building.           Numeracy CEC 11–12 (3.5)
Trigonometry has many real-world applications, including construction, navigation, astronomy, music theory, electrical engineering and manufacturing.Real-world applications
Trigonometry is used in constructing ramps, buildings and other structures that are constructed on sloped ground.Real-world applications

Considerations

  • The approximation of angles includes approximation to the nearest minute.
  • For problems involving applications of the sine rule where an angle is to be found, questions must inform students if the required angle is obtuse.
  • Students are not required to reproduce proofs of the sine, cosine and area rules.
  • Diagrams should be provided for problems involving angles of elevation and depression, and bearings, and for problems with two triangles.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities in Trigonometry

  • Angles are used by Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples in navigation, using both landmarks and celestial navigation. Connections

Course/Stage/Focus area

The mean and standard deviation are used to calculate z-scores.

Mathematics Standard Year 11 Data analysis

The normal distribution often describes natural phenomena, such as the distribution of heights, in a population.

Scientists use the normal distribution and z-scores to assess the significance of experimental results and make conclusions about hypotheses.

Real-world applications

The normal distribution is used in psychology, particularly in psychological testing and assessments. Test scores, such as IQ or standardised test results, are often distributed normally, and psychologists use this distribution to interpret scores.

z-scores are used in psychological research to analyse survey data, test scores and behavioural data, in order to draw conclusions and make psychological assessments.

Real-world applications

The normal distribution is applied in healthcare and medicine. For example, vital signs like blood pressure, cholesterol levels and body temperatures often follow a normal distribution, allowing healthcare professionals to set diagnostic thresholds and assess patient health.

Real-world applications

Engineers use the normal distribution in quality control and manufacturing processes. Deviations from a desired specification can be analysed using the normal distribution to ensure product quality.

Real-world applications

The normal distribution and z-scores are used in advanced data analysis, including hypothesis testing, confidence intervals and statistical inference.

Real-world applications
